extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning proof techniques, induction, and elementary set theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for writing and structuring proofs about closures, transitive closures, R^n, countability, and Cantor's diagonal argument; emphasizes use of recursion, induction, witness selection for existential claims, and explicit bijection constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitive-closure proof goals
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the definition of transitive closure we must prove three things: R ⊆ S, S is transitive, and for all T, if R ⊆ T ⊆ A × A and T is transitive, then S ⊆ T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give S a name (e.g., S = ⋃_{n≥1} R^n) at the beginning. Prove the three goals one at a time: (1) show R ⊆ S (often immediate from definition), (2) show S is transitive by taking arbitrary x,y,z and using existence of n,m with (x,y)∈R^n,(y,z)∈R^m and then Lemma R^{m+n}=R^m∘R^n to produce (x,z)∈R^{m+n}, (3) show minimality by letting arbitrary transitive T with R⊆T and proving by induction on n that R^n ⊆ T, hence S ⊆ T.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recursive definition of R^n
rubrics_metrics.description: Define R^1 = R; for every n > 1, R^{n+1} = R^n ∘ R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a definition uses an ellipsis or repeated composition, prefer a precise recursive definition. Use this recursive form directly when proving properties by induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma for compositions of powers: R^{m+n} = R^m ∘ R^n
rubrics_metrics.description: For all positive integers m and n, R^{m+n} = R^m ∘ R^n (proved by induction on n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove such equalities by fixing one index (e.g., m) and proceeding by induction on the other (n). Base case uses definition; induction step composes definitions and uses associativity of relation composition. State lemma explicitly and use it later (e.g., in transitivity proofs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving transitivity of a union S = ⋃_{n≥1} R^n
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove S is transitive: assume (x,y) ∈ S and (y,z) ∈ S, pick positive integers n,m with (x,y)∈R^n and (y,z)∈R^m, then use Lemma R^{n+m} = R^n ∘ R^m to conclude (x,z)∈R^{n+m} ⊆ S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce existential witnesses (n,m) immediately when you have membership in a union over n. The goal (x,z) ∈ S is existential, so produce the specific witness k = n + m and justify via the lemma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimality proof via induction on n
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove S ⊆ T for any transitive T with R ⊆ T, prove by induction on n that R^n ⊆ T (base n=1 uses R ⊆ T; induction step uses the recursive definition of R^{n+1} and transitivity of T).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take an arbitrary element of R^{n+1}, write it as composition (x,z) with (x,y)∈R and (y,z)∈R^n, use R ⊆ T and inductive hypothesis R^n ⊆ T to deduce both pairs lie in T, and then transitivity of T gives (x,z) ∈ T. Emphasize arbitrary choice to conclude inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof structure and naming
rubrics_metrics.description: It is convenient to give constructed sets names at the beginning of proofs (e.g., S = ⋃_{n≥1} R^n) and to state the high-level goals before proving them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List the separate goals implied by the definition being used and then address each goal in turn. If any part is routine (e.g., R ⊆ S), it may be left to the reader but mention that details can be filled in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using recursion together with induction
rubrics_metrics.description: When an object is defined recursively, proofs about it are naturally done by induction aligned with the recursive definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expand the recursive definition when needed in the inductive step so the inductive hypothesis can be applied directly; this is emphasized several times in relation to R^n and other recursively defined sequences/sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving existential statements by exhibiting a witness
rubrics_metrics.description: Existential goals (e.g., showing (x,z) ∈ S = ⋃ R^n) require finding and presenting an explicit witness (a specific n) that works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In transitivity proofs, choose k = n + m when combining (x,y) ∈ R^n and (y,z) ∈ R^m. Always state how the witness is obtained and reference lemmas that justify the membership claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure of a set under a function — two constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Closure of B under f can be obtained either (a) as the intersection of the family F = {C | B ⊆ C ⊆ A and C is closed under f}, or (b) as the union ⋃_{n≥1} B_n where B_1 = B and B_{n+1} = f(B_n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For (a) show F is nonempty and prove the intersection is closed and minimal; for (b) show each B_n ⊆ closure and that the union is closed under f and minimal. Present both constructions and prove they give the same smallest closed set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-ordering principle to obtain minimal witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the well-ordering principle to argue that, when S is a union of R^n and (a,b) ∈ S, there is a smallest positive integer n with (a,b)∈R^n; this defines distances and enables minimality arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define distance d(a,b) as the minimal n with (a,b)∈R^n and use its minimality in inequalities and decomposition arguments (e.g., split a path into two parts of prescribed lengths).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relating R^n to R-paths
rubrics_metrics.description: R^n = {(a,b) ∈ A×A | there is an R-path from a to b of length n}; similarly S (transitive closure) equals pairs for which there exists an R-path of some length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove these equalities, define R-paths as functions f: J_n → A with required edge conditions, prove equivalence by constructing paths from compositions and vice versa; use this viewpoint to reason about simple paths and bounds on n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving countability/equinumerosity
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a set A is countable/denumerable, either give a one-to-one onto function f : Z+ → A (denumerable) or show an onto map Z+ → A or a one-to-one map A → Z+ (equivalent characterizations in Theorem 7.1.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit constructions (examples given: map Z+→Z by parity encoding; Z+×Z+→Z+ enumerations) and apply Theorem 7.1.5. For finite sets, use unique n such that I_n ~ A. When constructing bijections, prove injectivity and surjectivity by cases or by giving explicit inverses where helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of countably many countable sets
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is a countable family of countable sets (F = {A_1,A_2,...}), then ⋃F is countable: define f : Z+×Z+ → ⋃F by f(n,m) = the m-th element of A_n, then compose with a bijection Z+→Z+×Z+ to get an onto map Z+→⋃F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handle empty family or empty members separately (remove empty set from family if necessary). The construction requires lists for each A_n and a listing of the family; the composed function is then onto.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countability of finite sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of all finite sequences over a countable set A is countable: for each n let S_n be sequences of length n, show S_{n+1} ~ S_n × A, and then ⋃_{n≥0} S_n is countable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove S_{n+1} ~ S_n × A by the natural append operation (verify bijectivity), use induction on n to show each S_n is countable, and apply countable-union theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor diagonal argument for uncountability of P(Z+)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show P(Z+) is uncountable: assume arbitrary f : Z+ → P(Z+); define D = {n ∈ Z+ | n ∉ f(n)} and prove D ∈ P(Z+) but D ≠ f(n) for every n, hence f is not onto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the construction heuristically as choosing D to differ from each f(n) in the n-th position (diagonal), then formalize via case analysis on whether n ∈ f(n) to show D differs from f(n). Emphasize that the definition of D guarantees D ∉ Ran(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving functions injective/surjective — case analysis and inverses
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a function is injective or surjective, use direct arguments (case splits when function is defined piecewise) or provide an explicit inverse function when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: parity-based map f: Z+→Z used cases 'if n is even then f(n)=n/2 else f(n)=(1−n)/2' — prove injectivity by separating even/odd cases, surjectivity by providing preimage formulas for positive/negative integers. When possible, cite Theorems about inverse functions to conclude bijectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard proof techniques emphasized
rubrics_metrics.description: Use arbitrary-element method for inclusions, case analysis when definitions are piecewise, induction for statements parameterized by n, and naming and structuring proofs into clear subgoals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout examples, adopt the patterns: let variables be arbitrary, assume hypotheses, produce required membership or equality, and conclude; if some routine part is omitted, note that readers should work out the details.
